title: The Carbon Footprint of the Built World

zones.label: Built Environment Share (Architecture 2030)
zones.summary: Architecture 2030 attributes about 42% of annual global CO2 emissions to the built environment, shown as a slice pulled out of the whole ring.
facts: Architecture 2030 puts the built environment at about 42% of annual global CO2 emissions (Architecture 2030, Why the Built Environment).
That 42% is the sum of two parts: about 27% from building operations and about 15% from embodied carbon (Architecture 2030).
Buildings are one of the largest single levers for cutting emissions, which is why a whole chapter of this book is about materials (Chapter 20).
This panel uses only the Architecture 2030 accounting. The UNEP numbers sit in their own panel because they draw the boundary differently.

zones.label: Operational Carbon (Architecture 2030)
zones.summary: About 27% of annual global CO2 comes from running buildings: heating, cooling, lighting, hot water, and equipment.
facts: Architecture 2030 attributes approximately 27% of annual global CO2 emissions to building operations (Architecture 2030).
Operational carbon is the emissions from the energy a building uses every year it is occupied (Chapter 19).
It is spread over decades and can shrink as the electric grid gets cleaner or the building is retrofitted (Chapter 20).
Better insulation, air sealing, and efficient equipment cut this slice for the life of the building.

zones.label: Embodied Carbon (Architecture 2030)
zones.summary: About 15% more comes from the carbon built into materials and construction before anyone moves in.
facts: Architecture 2030 counts an additional 15% of annual global CO2 emissions as embodied carbon, tied to materials such as cement, iron, steel, and aluminum (Architecture 2030).
Embodied carbon is front-loaded: nearly all of it is emitted before the building opens, so it cannot be fixed later (Chapter 20).
As buildings become more efficient to operate, materials make up a larger share of a building's life-cycle emissions (Chapter 20).
Choosing a lower-carbon material or using less of it is the main way a designer cuts this slice.

zones.label: UNEP GlobalABC Accounting
zones.summary: A separate accounting: the UNEP and GlobalABC 2024/2025 report puts buildings and construction at 32% of global energy and 34% of global CO2.
facts: The UNEP and GlobalABC Global Status Report for Buildings and Construction 2024/2025 reports 32% of global energy use and 34% of global CO2 emissions.
These figures cover the buildings and construction sector as UNEP and GlobalABC define it, which reaches beyond building operations to include construction and materials.
34% and Architecture 2030's 42% are not competing answers to one question. They come from different studies with different boundaries.
Never add, average, or swap these numbers with the Architecture 2030 numbers. Quote each with its source.

zones.label: Materials Behind Embodied Carbon
zones.summary: A skyline built from cement, steel, aluminum, timber, glass, and insulation: each material carries a different carbon cost.
facts: Architecture 2030 ties embodied carbon to materials such as cement, iron, steel, and aluminum (Architecture 2030).
Cement releases carbon dioxide from the limestone itself, regardless of the fuel burned in the kiln (Chapter 20).
Per kilogram, concrete is low in embodied energy, steel is higher, and primary aluminum is far higher, but total impact is intensity times quantity (Chapter 20).
Timber can store carbon, and cement substitutes and recycled content lower a mix's footprint; confirm claims with a product EPD (Chapter 20).

zones.label: New Floor Area, 2020 to 2060
zones.summary: The world is expected to add about 2.6 trillion square feet (241 billion square meters) of floor area between 2020 and 2060.
facts: Architecture 2030 projects about 2.6 trillion ft2 (241 billion m2) of new floor area added to the global building stock from 2020 to 2060, using International Energy Agency data.
Architecture 2030 compares that to adding a New York City's worth of floor area every month for 40 years.
Architecture 2030, citing United Nations data, says three-quarters of the infrastructure that will exist in 2050 has yet to be built.
Most of that building is still a decision: the materials chosen in the next few decades set the embodied carbon (Chapter 20).

zones.label: Different Boundaries, Different Numbers
zones.summary: Two reputable sources give different shares because they draw the boundary differently, so always ask what a number counts.
facts: Architecture 2030 reports 42% for the built environment; UNEP and GlobalABC report 34% for buildings and construction. Each is correct for its own boundary and method.
A third example: RICS cites a UNEP estimate that for 2021 about 28% of global CO2 was operational and about 12% embodied, a different year and boundary again.
Before using any share, check what it counts (operations, materials, construction), the year, and the data source.
State the source next to the number, and keep numbers from different sources in separate sentences.

quiz.question: Which region shows the slice pulled out of the full ring, about 42% of annual global CO2 in Architecture 2030's accounting?
quiz.explanation: Architecture 2030 sums operations (about 27%) and embodied carbon (about 15%) to roughly 42% of annual global CO2 emissions.

quiz.question: Which part of the pulled-out slice covers the emissions from the energy used to heat, cool, and light buildings year after year?
quiz.explanation: That is operating energy, about 27% of annual global CO2 in the Architecture 2030 figures.

quiz.question: A designer swaps a high-carbon material for a lower-carbon one before construction. Which part of the Architecture 2030 slice does this reduce?
quiz.explanation: Material choice changes the carbon built into the building, about 15% of annual global CO2 in the Architecture 2030 figures.

quiz.question: A report states that buildings and construction use 32% of global energy and produce 34% of global CO2. Which region holds that accounting?
quiz.explanation: These are the UNEP and GlobalABC 2024/2025 figures, kept apart from Architecture 2030's numbers because the boundaries differ.

quiz.question: Which region shows the stacked blocks of cement, steel, aluminum, timber, glass, and insulation?
quiz.explanation: These are the materials whose manufacture creates embodied carbon, each with a different footprint per kilogram and per building.

quiz.question: Which region shows the long bar of repeating small city icons, standing for roughly 241 billion square meters of floor area added over 40 years?
quiz.explanation: Architecture 2030 projects about 2.6 trillion square feet of new floor area from 2020 to 2060.

quiz.question: A reader quotes 42% from one source and 34% from another and says one of them must be wrong. Which region explains why they can both be right?
quiz.explanation: Different studies count different things and use different methods, so the shares differ. Each must be quoted with its own source.

quiz.question: Which region would you use to explain why most of a building's embodied carbon is already emitted by the day the doors open?
quiz.explanation: Embodied carbon is front-loaded: manufacture, transport, and construction all happen before occupancy.

quiz.question: Which region warns that three-quarters of the infrastructure that will exist in 2050 has not been built yet?
quiz.explanation: Architecture 2030, citing United Nations data, uses this to show that today's design choices lock in decades of emissions.

quiz.question: Which region would you point to when someone asks whether the 27% and the 34% figures can be added together or compared directly?
quiz.explanation: They come from different sources with different boundaries, so they should never be mixed in a single number.
